feedback: If a learner says acceleration means 'going fast', contrast a fast STEADY speed (no acceleration) with a slow speeding-up (acceleration): acceleration means the speed is increasing, deceleration means it is decreasing, and steady speed (however fast) is neither.
If a learner treats 'resultant' as an extra force, re-show the two unequal pulls and the single combined arrow — the resultant is the net effect of the forces already there, not an additional one.

If a learner says 'balanced forces' means there are no forces, point to a tug-of-war where both sides pull equally and it stays at a standstill: two real pulls are acting, they just cancel to a zero resultant. (Equal pulls give balance and zero resultant; unequal pulls give a net resultant.)
If a learner confuses lever/fulcrum/moment, label the pivot (fulcrum), the bar (lever) and the turning effect (moment) separately on the see-saw.
activities.intendedInsight: Each abstract term becomes learnable when tied to something you can see AND to a non-example that fences off the usual confusion: acceleration is not just 'fast', a resultant is not an added force, and balanced does not mean no forces.
learnerActions: Study one rich force-and-motion scene containing a cart that is speeding up, a see-saw, and a tug-of-war.
For each key term, state a student-friendly meaning in your own words, point to the part of the scene it labels, give one example, and give one non-example.
For 'fulcrum', identify the see-saw pivot and say why it is not the load and not the effort — it is the point the lever turns on.

For 'acceleration', show several positions of the cart taken at equal time intervals, with the gaps between them getting progressively larger so the increasing speed is visible (not merely that the cart is fast), and contrast it with 'deceleration' (gaps shrinking, slowing down) and 'constant speed' (equal gaps, no change).

For 'resultant', look at a tug-of-war in which one side pulls harder than the other, draw the single combined arrow that shows the net, and explain that it is not an extra pull but the net of the two.

Build a Frayer-style organiser for 2–3 high-leverage words (term, meaning, a drawing, examples, non-examples); at the primary end, use a drawing in place of 'characteristics' and synonyms/antonyms for examples/non-examples.
activities.title: Pin each word to a scene, then fence it with a non-example

feedback: If a learner labels the steady-speed stage 'accelerating', point out the speed is not changing, so there is no acceleration during that stage.

If a learner expects the object to instantly travel in the push direction, explain that a resultant sets how motion changes, not an instant jump: from rest the object starts moving in the resultant's direction and builds up gradually, and an object that is already moving keeps its motion while the resultant gradually bends its path or speeds/slows it.
When introducing the resultant, start the object from rest where possible so the link between resultant direction and the change in motion is cleanest.
activities.intendedInsight: The relational, dynamic terms (acceleration, deceleration, resultant) are clearer when you watch the effect they name unfold, not just read a definition — and the resultant sets how the motion changes, not an instant jump to the push direction.
learnerActions: Watch the cart start from rest and speed up, then move at a steady speed, then slow to a stop; name the stage with 'acceleration', 'constant speed' and 'deceleration' as each happens.

Combine two arrows of different sizes and directions acting on an object that starts from rest, and watch the single resultant arrow that results; describe which way it points and how the object's motion changes from rest.
Contrast a steady glide (constant speed, no acceleration) with a speeding-up motion (acceleration) and say what is different about the speed in each.
activities.title: See the dynamic words happen

feedback: For a sorting error, re-ask whether the speed is changing: changing speed is accelerating or decelerating; unchanging speed is constant.
If a learner can select the right word but cannot use it in a sentence, prompt them to say the same idea in their own words so recognition becomes production.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated retrieval in different contexts strengthens word knowledge and the ability to recognise where each term belongs.
learnerActions: Match each term to its student-friendly definition.
Sort short motion descriptions or clips into 'accelerating', 'decelerating' or 'constant speed'.
Complete sentences by choosing and inserting the correct term, then read the full sentence aloud.
Revisit the vocabulary over the unit, adding each term to a vocabulary wall anchored to a motion image or force-arrow diagram, and use the words again in later lessons.
activities.title: Consolidate with retrieval across varied contexts

feedback: Expected accurate use: at rest and at steady speed the forces are balanced (zero resultant, no change in motion); pushing off from rest, forces are unbalanced with a resultant forwards causing acceleration; braking while moving forwards, unbalanced with a resultant backwards causing deceleration; 'speed' is how fast, and acceleration (speeding up) is distinguished from deceleration (slowing).

If steady speed is called 'unbalanced' because 'it's moving', correct it: steady speed means no change in motion, so the forces are balanced with zero resultant — reserve 'unbalanced' for changing motion.
If 'balanced' is used only for a stationary object, model using 'balanced' for BOTH the at-rest stage and the constant-speed stage.

If 'moment' is treated as an instant of time, re-anchor it to the turning effect of a force on a lever; if 'mechanical advantage' or 'force' drifts to an everyday meaning, contrast the everyday and scientific senses explicitly.
activities.intendedInsight: A word is only truly learned when it does real work in explaining and predicting, not when a definition has been copied.
learnerActions: Explain a chosen term in your own words to a partner and justify an example you pick.
Use 'moment', 'lever' and 'fulcrum' to describe how a see-saw works.
Explain why a longer spanner helps turn a tight bolt, using the word 'moment'.
Give a sentence using 'mechanical advantage' about a bottle opener or a wheelbarrow.

Talk through a whole journey — waiting at rest, pushing off and speeding up, then steady speed, then braking to a stop — saying at each stage whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced and what the resultant force is doing.
activities.title: Explain it back and use the words to describe real cases
